paras: The Cherokee mobilization against Creek freedmen at Fort Gibson was an armed gathering of several hundred Cherokees in early August 1880 that demanded the surrender of thirteen Black men of the Creek Nation and threatened to go after them. The thirteen were accused of crossing into the Cherokee Nation and shooting two Cherokee youths, Cobb and Cowan, to avenge the hanging of two Creek Black men. A council at Muskogee defused the confrontation on August 4; the story ran nationally as a clash of 'Creek negroes' and Cherokees.

In late July two Creek Black men accused of stealing livestock were hanged near Gibson Station. A Vinita dispatch named them Manlay and Jones and blamed, 'it is supposed', Texas cattlemen; the Little Rock wire named them Bill Peters and Long Monday and blamed 'Cherokee lynchers'. Black men of the Creek Nation blamed the Cherokees.

According to the Vinita correspondent, thirteen Black men crossed into the Cherokee side on Tuesday morning, 'swearing they would kill the first Cherokee they met'. They fired on two Cherokee boys returning from Gibson; Cowan was wounded in the face and carried off by his horse, while Cobb fought back and was shot down near his uncle's house, dying three hours later. The Little Rock wire put the crossing on Wednesday, called Cowan 'fatally wounded', and added that Dick Glass, 'a Creek', was also killed in the fight, without saying who killed him.

The Cherokees then demanded the thirteen from the Creek Chief and gave him until that night to surrender them, declaring that otherwise they would go after them. The Vinita dispatch counted 300 armed men on the ground with more arriving, and expected a battle against Black men 'about 200 strong and well armed'. Cherokee chiefs, Bushyhead with Adair or with Ross depending on the account, had difficulty holding the gathering back and won a suspension of hostilities only on the promise that the thirteen be delivered. A Chicago Times special said the Cherokees declared their intention of 'driving out every black in the nation'.

On August 4 a Creek-Cherokee council at Muskogee agreed that the Creeks would arrest Cobb's killers wherever found in their jurisdiction. A joint commission of two Creeks and two Cherokees was to decide whether Cobb died on Cherokee or Creek soil, and so which nation would try the accused; the Cherokees were to disband. None of the accused had yet been arrested; a St. Louis report called the arrangement a compromise in which the Creeks would surrender the men.

A week later a brief item reported that the Cherokees and the Creek Black men, 'recently at war', had negotiated a peace with the Creek Indians as mediators. The Little Rock wire also noted a white man reported killed, which would 'require the interference' of federal authorities, without details. No report of a trial of the accused was found in the coverage.

The story reached the white press through two wire streams: a Cincinnati Commercial special from Vinita, printed from August 5 in the Wheeling Register, Chicago Tribune and Richmond Dispatch, and a Little Rock dispatch that ran from August 7 into mid-August Minnesota weeklies. Both streams called the Cherokees' targets 'negroes' or 'Creek negroes', under headlines such as 'Vengeance', 'Creek vs. Cherokee' and 'Negroes and Indians', and the Vinita special called them 'these black devils'.

Editorial comment sided with the Cherokees. The Chicago Times special, reprinted in the Dallas Herald, blamed a 'Black Terror band' of cattle thieves, joked that the hanged men were found 'enjoying a swing', and concluded that the affair would open the territory to white settlement, 'which should be done'. The New York Sun wrote that 'the color line was disastrously drawn' and that the Creeks had 'wisely' agreed to give up the Black men for trial and punishment. No coverage in the Black press was found.

Accounts differed on the toll: the detailed Vinita report had Cowan wounded and escaping, the Little Rock wire called him fatally wounded, and condensed Commercial summaries said both boys were killed. They also differed on the size of the Cherokee force, 300 or about 200, and on whether Texas cattlemen or Cherokees carried out the earlier hanging.

reader.title: Cherokee mobilization against Creek freedmen at Fort Gibson
bases: Several hundred armed Cherokees gathered at Fort Gibson and threatened to cross into the Creek Nation after thirteen Black Creek men unless they were surrendered, but no attack on them is reported (A1, A2, A8, A9).

Separate dispatches from Vinita (A1, A2), Muskogee (A8) and Fort Smith via Little Rock (A9) agree that armed Cherokees assembled near Gibson demanding thirteen Black Creek men after the shooting of Cobb and Cowan.

accounts.label: Vinita dispatch (Cincinnati Commercial)
accounts.gist: Two Creek Black cattle thieves were hanged July 26, supposedly by Texas cattlemen; Creek Black men blamed the Cherokees, thirteen crossed vowing to kill the first Cherokee met, wounded Cowan and killed Cobb; 300 armed Cherokees demanded the thirteen.

accounts.label: Little Rock wire from Fort Smith
accounts.gist: The hanged men were Bill Peters and Long Monday, killed by 'Cherokee lynchers' July 27; Cobb was killed, Cowan fatally wounded and Dick Glass, a Creek, killed; 200 Cherokees at Fort Gibson held back by their chiefs pending delivery of the thirteen.

accounts.label: Muskogee council report
accounts.gist: The Creeks agreed to arrest Cobb's killers; a joint commission would decide jurisdiction and the Cherokees would disband.

accounts.label: Chicago Times special from Parsons, Kan.
accounts.gist: A 'Black Terror band' of Creek Black men ran off Cherokee cattle; Cherokees caught and hanged two; the band took vengeance, both Cherokees died, and the Cherokees vowed to drive out every Black resident.

framing.detail: The Vinita special called the Black men 'these black devils' and headlined the story 'Vengeance' and 'Battle Imminent Between Negroes and Indians'.
The Chicago Times special portrayed a thieving 'Black Terror band', joked about the hanged men 'enjoying a swing', and urged opening the territory to white settlement.
The Little Rock wire ran in the Midwest under 'Creek vs. Cherokee' and 'Indian Troubles', describing the hanged men as horse thieves.
The New York Sun saw 'the color line' drawn and said the Creeks 'wisely' gave the Black men up for punishment.

record_check.dossier: The shooting was Tuesday (Aug. 3) per the Vinita dispatch or Wednesday per the Little Rock wire; the gathering ran Aug. 3-4 and the council settled terms Aug. 4.
The targets of the Cherokee threat were thirteen unnamed Creek Black men; Dick Glass, 'a Creek' of unstated race, died in the earlier fight, killer not named.
Cherokees, a gathering of 200-300 armed men.
No Black death is attributed to the Cherokee gathering; Glass's race is not stated.
No Black person is reported injured; the wounded Cowan was a Cherokee.
Cobb and Glass killed; Cowan wounded, 'fatally wounded' or killed by account; a white man reported killed separately.

Cherokees assembled at Fort Gibson, near the Cherokee-Creek line; the shooting was near Gibson Station.
